sections.title: Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions Using Identities

slides.title: A Curious Square Pattern
slides.kicker: Numbers that keep a secret promise
bullets: Pick any three consecutive square numbers, like 1, 4 and 9.
Add the smallest and the largest: 1 + 9 = 10.
Subtract twice the middle square: 10 - (2 × 4) = 10 - 8 = 2.

items: Add the smallest and the largest

slides.note: Pattern number one. Yeh toh hamesha 2 hi deta hai!

slides.title: Try It Again, Get 2
slides.kicker: Two more tries, same stubborn answer
bullets: The book repeats the game with many sets of three consecutive squares, and the result always seems to be 2.
slides.note: Same answer every single time. Suspicious, right?

slides.title: Why Always 2?
slides.kicker: A mystery this chapter will solve
bullets: The pattern may look surprising, but the book promises to uncover the reason behind it using algebra.
Algebraic identities are special mathematical rules that make it easier to simplify complicated calculations.
They also help us work efficiently with algebraic expressions.
slides.note: Hold that question in your head. Section 4.3 cracks it open.

slides.title: Your Next Step Up
bullets: In earlier chapters you learnt about linear polynomials and linear equations, and how they describe relationships between quantities.
This chapter takes the next step: exploring algebraic identities.
Think and Reflect invites you to test 4 consecutive squares and hunt for your own pattern.
slides.note: Explorers first, provers later. That is the chapter's way.

slides.title: One Square, Four Pieces
slides.kicker: Draw the identity instead of memorising it
bullets: Join segments of length a and b to make a segment of length (a + b) units, then build a square of that side.
The outer square has area (a + b)^2.
Inside it sit a larger square of area a^2, a smaller square of area b^2, and two rectangles of area ab each.
Together the four pieces fill the big square, so (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2.
slides.note: The picture is the proof, at least when a and b are lengths.

slides.title: Does It Survive Negatives?
bullets: Line segments cannot have negative length, so the book checks numbers that are not lengths.
Let a = -2 and b = -3. Then (a + b) = -5, so (a + b)^2 = 25.
Both sides agree, so the identity works again.
slides.note: Minus signs behave perfectly here. Good.

slides.title: Rationals Join the Test
bullets: Both sides match, so the identity seems true for rational numbers too.
slides.note: Still not every number though. One more push needed.

slides.title: The Distributive Proof
slides.kicker: One line of algebra settles it
bullets: Checking samples is never enough, so the book investigates using the distributive property of numbers.
Expanding gives a^2 + ab + ba + b^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, since ab = ba.
Now the identity is certain for all numbers, not just the ones we tried.
slides.note: Testing is guessing. Distributing is proving.

slides.title: Equation or Identity?
bullets: In Grade 8 you were introduced to (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 as an identity.
An algebraic identity is an equation that is true for all values of the variables occurring in it.
An ordinary equation need not be true for all values.
That is exactly why the book tested negatives and rationals before proving.
slides.note: Identity: always true. Equation: only sometimes true.

slides.title: Factoring By Matching
bullets: The identity (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 can also be used to find factors of some algebraic expressions.
Check that the first and last terms are perfect squares.
Check that the middle term is twice the product of their square roots.
Then read off a and b, and the whole expression collapses into (a + b)^2.

items: Spot perfect squares at the ends

slides.note: Reading the identity backwards, piece by piece.

slides.title: Factoring x^2 + 4x + 4
slides.kicker: Example 5: a perfect square in disguise
bullets: We observe that x^2 = (x)^2 and 4 = 2^2, while the middle term 4x = 2(x)(2).
So x^2 + 4x + 4 can be compared with a^2 + 2ab + b^2, where a = x and b = 2.
We conclude that x^2 + 4x + 4 = (x + 2)^2.
Therefore (x + 2) is a factor of x^2 + 4x + 4.
slides.note: Three terms, one square. Sweet and quick.

slides.title: Factoring 36x^2 + 12x + 1
bullets: Write the ends as squares: 36x^2 = (6x)^2 and 1 = 1^2.
The middle term fits too: 12x = 2(6x)(1).
Thus (6x + 1) is a factor of 36x^2 + 12x + 1.
slides.note: That little 1 was a perfect square all along.

slides.title: Common Factor First
bullets: In 50p^2 + 60pq + 18q^2, a term whose square is 50p^2 would be 50p, needing a square root symbol.
To avoid that, notice 2 is a common factor of 50p^2, 60pq and 18q^2.
Now (5p)^2 = 25p^2 and (3q)^2 = 9q^2, so the bracket is (5p + 3q)^2 and the answer is 2(5p + 3q)^2.
slides.note: No square root symbol needed. Clean move.

slides.title: The Minus Twin
slides.kicker: Replace b by -b in the identity
bullets: Think and Reflect asks: what if we replace b by -b in (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2?
We get (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2.
This is also an identity and can be used in ways similar to the plus version.
slides.note: One sign flip, a whole new tool in the kit.

slides.title: Case Closed: It Is 2
bullets: Any three consecutive numbers can be taken as (n - 1), n and (n + 1); their squares are (n - 1)^2, n^2 and (n + 1)^2.
Using the identities, (n - 1)^2 + (n + 1)^2 = n^2 - 2n + 1 + n^2 + 2n + 1 = 2n^2 + 2.
Subtracting twice the middle square, 2n^2, leaves exactly 2.
This is a proof that you always arrive at 2, for every n.
slides.note: The 4.1 mystery, solved with two identities.

slides.title: A Rectangle of Factors
slides.kicker: Multiply x + 3 by x + 4 with tiles
bullets: A rectangle with sides x + 3 and x + 4 units has area (x + 3)(x + 4) sq units.
Using distributivity: (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 3x + 4x + 12.
Combining the middle terms gives x^2 + 7x + 12.
Algebra tiles now let us see this whole product with our eyes.
slides.note: Area is just a friendlier word for multiply.

slides.title: Reading The Tile Picture
bullets: The expression x + 3 is one x-tile plus three unit tiles; x + 4 is one x-tile plus four unit tiles.
Their product fills an inner rectangle holding the x^2-tile, 7 x-tiles and 12 unit tiles.
The 7x has been split as 3x + 4x: three x-tiles sit on the right of the x^2-tile and four below it.
The 12 unit tiles form a 3 by 4 array, so the rectangle's dimensions are x + 3 and x + 4.
slides.note: The picture literally shows the factors.

slides.title: One Picture, Two Powers
slides.kicker: Multiply and factor with the same tiles
bullets: Multiplication view: the linear expressions x + 3 and x + 4 multiply to give (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 7x + 12.
Factorisation view: x^2 + 7x + 12 factors into the linear factors (x + 3) and (x + 4).
Same rectangular arrangement, read in two directions.
Think and Reflect: if 7x is split as 2x + 5x instead, can a similar rectangle form? Check other possibilities too.
slides.note: Ek picture, do kaam. That is the beauty of tiles.

slides.title: The General Pattern
bullets: The book shows (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 7x + 12 and (x + 6)(x + 7) = x^2 + 13x + 42.
Spot the pattern: 7 = 3 + 4 and 12 = 3 × 4; then 13 = 6 + 7 and 42 = 6 × 7.
Generalising: (x + a)(x + b) = x^2 + (a + b)x + ab.
Think and Reflect: lay out tiles for x^2 + 11x + 30 so that you can see its factors.
slides.note: a + b in the middle, ab at the end.

slides.title: When x Gets Company
bullets: For a rectangle with sidelengths 2x + 3 and 3x + 1, the area is (2x + 3)(3x + 1).
Distributivity gives 6x^2 + 2x + 9x + 3 = 6x^2 + 11x + 3.
The book's fill-in-the-blank generalises it: (px + a)(qx + b) = (pq)x^2 + (pb + aq)x + ab.
Verify your answer using the distributive property, exactly as the book asks.
slides.note: Bigger tiles, same rectangle logic.

slides.title: Fractions With Algebra
bullets: A rational algebraic expression is a fraction whose numerator and denominator are algebraic expressions.
To simplify it, we cancel the common factors between the expressions in the numerator and denominator.
That means factorising both parts first, and our identities do that job.
Example 16 simplifies (x^2 - 7x + 12) / (5x^2 + 5x - 100), assuming 5x^2 + 5x - 100 is not 0.
slides.note: Identities doing the heavy lifting again.

slides.title: Splitting The Numerator
slides.kicker: Find a and b: sum -7, product 12
bullets: For the numerator x^2 - 7x + 12, we need a and b such that a + b = -7 and ab = 12.
Can you think of two such numbers? They are -3 and -4.
So factorising gives x^2 - 7x + 12 = (x - 3)(x - 4).
slides.note: Sum and product are the two clues. Always.

slides.title: Tidying The Denominator
bullets: In 5x^2 + 5x - 100, all three terms are multiples of 5.
Take 5 as a common factor: 5x^2 + 5x - 100 = 5(x^2 + x - 20).
Now find a and b with a + b = 1 and ab = -20. They are 5 and -4.
slides.note: Tidy first, split second. Order matters.

slides.title: Cancel With Care
slides.kicker: The payoff, plus one safety rule
bullets: Substituting the factored forms, the fraction becomes (x - 4)(x - 3) / 5(x - 4)(x + 5).
The common factor x - 4 can be cancelled because it is not equal to 0.
We know that because 5x^2 + 5x - 100 is not 0, as Example 16 assumes.
The simplified result is (x - 3) / 5(x + 5).
slides.note: Cancelling is legal only when the factor is not zero.

flashcards.back: (a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2, and it works in ways similar to the plus version.

quiz.q: For the squares 1, 4, 9, the book computes (1 + 9) - (2 × 4). What is the result?
Using the same pattern on 9, 16, 25, what is (9 + 25) - (2 × 16)?
quiz.why: 34 - 32 = 2; the book finds this same result for every set of three consecutive squares.

Add only the two middle squares

quiz.why: The figure shows two rectangles of area ab each; together they make 2ab.

quiz.why: (a + b) = 1/12 so its square is 1/144, and 4/9 - 1 + 9/16 also gives 1/144.

options: Checking samples cannot cover every number

quiz.why: x^2 + 4x + 4 = x^2 + 2(x)(2) + 2^2 fits the plus form with a = x and b = 2.

quiz.why: The book writes 36x^2 = (6x)^2 and 12x = 2(6x)(1), so a = 6x and b = 1.

quiz.q: In the tile rectangle for x^2 + 7x + 12, how are the 12 unit tiles arranged?
quiz.why: The book places the 12 unit tiles in a 3 by 4 array, matching sides x + 3 and x + 4.

quiz.q: From the Think and Reflect, (x + 2)(x + 3) equals...
quiz.why: 2 + 3 = 5 gives the middle term and 2 × 3 = 6 the constant.

quiz.q: The area of the rectangle with sides 2x + 3 and 3x + 1 is...
Which two numbers have product 12 and sum -7, as needed for x^2 - 7x + 12?
What is the first move on the denominator 5x^2 + 5x - 100?
quiz.why: All three terms are multiples of 5, so the book takes out 5 to get 5(x^2 + x - 20).

quiz.q: After factorising and cancelling, Example 16 leaves which simplified expression?
quiz.why: Cancelling the common factor (x - 4) leaves (x - 3) over 5(x + 5).

quiz.q: From the Think and Reflect, 36s^2 - 12st + t^2 equals...
quiz.why: It matches a^2 - 2ab + b^2 with a = 6s and b = t, using the minus twin identity.

quiz.q: Saira's picture: a square of side x, 8 strips of x by 1, and 15 unit squares. Which expression is the total area?
quiz.why: One x^2 square plus 8 strips of area x plus 15 unit squares adds to x^2 + 8x + 15.

examples.title: The Always-2 Mystery, Proven
examples.problem: Show that for any three consecutive square numbers, adding the smallest and largest and subtracting twice the middle square always gives 2.
steps: Let the three consecutive numbers be (n - 1), n and (n + 1), so their squares are (n - 1)^2, n^2 and (n + 1)^2.
Expand the outer squares with the identities: (n - 1)^2 = n^2 - 2n + 1 and (n + 1)^2 = n^2 + 2n + 1.
Add the smallest and largest squares: n^2 - 2n + 1 + n^2 + 2n + 1 = 2n^2 + 2.
examples.answer: The result is 2 for every n, which proves the pattern from Example 1.

examples.title: Factoring With a Common Factor First
steps: A term whose square is 50p^2 would be 50p, which drags in a square root symbol, so look for a common factor first.
The number 2 is a common factor of 50p^2, 60pq and 18q^2, so write the expression as 2(25p^2 + 30pq + 9q^2).
Match the bracket with a^2 + 2ab + b^2: 25p^2 = (5p)^2, 30pq = 2(5p)(3q) and 9q^2 = (3q)^2, so a = 5p and b = 3q.

examples.title: A Tile Rectangle With Bigger Sides
examples.problem: Find the area of a rectangle with sides 2x + 3 and 3x + 1, and state the general rule for (px + a)(qx + b) that the book's fill-in-the-blank builds.
steps: Combine the middle terms: 2x + 9x = 11x, so the area is 6x^2 + 11x + 3 sq units.
In general, (px + a)(qx + b) = (pq)x^2 + (pb + aq)x + ab, which the book asks you to verify using distributivity.
examples.answer: The area is 6x^2 + 11x + 3, and (px + a)(qx + b) = (pq)x^2 + (pb + aq)x + ab.

examples.title: Taming a Rational Expression
examples.problem: Simplify (x^2 - 7x + 12) / (5x^2 + 5x - 100), assuming 5x^2 + 5x - 100 is not equal to 0.
steps: Numerator: find a and b with a + b = -7 and ab = 12. They are -3 and -4, so x^2 - 7x + 12 = (x - 3)(x - 4).
Denominator: all three terms are multiples of 5, so 5x^2 + 5x - 100 = 5(x^2 + x - 20).
In the bracket, find a and b with a + b = 1 and ab = -20. They are 5 and -4, so the denominator is 5(x - 4)(x + 5).
Write the fraction as (x - 4)(x - 3) / 5(x - 4)(x + 5) and cancel the common factor (x - 4); it is not 0 because the denominator is assumed not 0.

steps.detail: True for all values of the variables, unlike an ordinary equation.

steps.detail: Fit expressions to a^2 + 2ab + b^2 or a^2 - 2ab + b^2 and read the factors.
